title: Where, and what
prompt:
Most error messages have two halves. Click the part of this one that tells
you *what* went wrong.
hint: One part names the code R was running. The other describes the problem.

options.feedback:
Right. After the colon is the *what*: R couldn't find a package by that
name — here because it's misspelled. Before the colon is the *where*:
the call R was running when it stopped.

Reading them in that order — what, then where — is the quickest way
into any error. The *what* tells you the kind of problem; the *where*
tells you which line to look at.

This is the *where*: the call R was running when it stopped. Useful for
finding the line, but the description of the problem comes after the
colon.

Every error starts this way — it's just R announcing an error. The
useful parts come after it: which call, and then what went wrong.

title: A bracket that never closes
prompt:
This gives `Error: unexpected end of input` — R reached the end of the
line still waiting for a bracket to close. Fix it so it works out each
patient's MAP.

MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3
hint:
Count the brackets that open and the brackets that close. Then think about
*where* the missing one goes — the division should apply to the whole top
part of the formula.
setup:
patients <- data.frame(
  age        = c(67, 54, 71, 48, 62),
  blood_type = c("A+", "O-", "B+", "O+", "A-"),
  sbp        = c(142, 118, NA, 131, 156),
  discharged = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  dbp        = c(88, 76, 82, 84, 94)
)

solution.why:
The missing bracket goes after `patients$dbp`, so the division by 3
applies to the whole of `sbp + 2 × dbp`. R can read the line now, and
the formula is the one you wanted.

checks.on_fail:
The MAPs aren't right yet. Check that the division applies to the
whole of the top part of the formula.

misconceptions.feedback:
There's still a bracket that never closes. Count them: every `(` needs
a `)`.

No error now — R can read the line — but look at the answer: 200.67 for
a patient at 142/88. The bracket closes in the wrong place, so only the
diastolic part is divided by 3. That's the same mistake from module 9.

This is worth sitting with. Fixing an error means R can run your code.
It doesn't mean the code does what you meant. That's module 14.

title: What ran before it stopped
prompt:
This stops with an error on the third line:

```r
weight <- 70
height <- "1.75"
bmi <- weight / (height * height)
```

```
Error in height * height : non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

Afterwards, which of these exist?
hint:
R runs a script one line at a time, top to bottom. What had already
happened when it reached the third line?

options.feedback:
Right. R runs line by line, and stops at the first error. Everything
before it has already happened — `weight` and `height` were stored.
The line that failed stored nothing, so `bmi` doesn't exist.

That matters when you re-run part of a script: some things will already
be there from last time, and some won't.

options.text: None of them — the script failed
options.feedback:
A script isn't all-or-nothing. The first two lines ran and stored their
values before R reached the error.

An error doesn't give you an `NA` — it stops. The line that failed
stored nothing at all, so `bmi` doesn't exist.

title: Where it broke, and why
prompt:
The error names `height * height`, on the third line. Click the line that
actually *caused* it.

```
Error in height * height : non-numeric argument to binary operator
```
hint:
"Non-numeric argument" means one side of the `*` isn't a number. Why isn't
it?

options.feedback:
Right. The quotes made `height` text, back on the second line. R only
noticed on the third, when it tried to multiply.

That's the general rule: an error tells you where R *noticed* the
problem, which isn't always where the problem *is*. When the line it
names looks fine, look at where its ingredients came from.

This is where R *noticed* the problem, and it's the line the error
names. But the formula is fine. It was handed text instead of a number
— so where did that text come from?
`weight` is a proper number. The other ingredient is the problem.

title: A warning isn't an error
prompt:
```r
labs <- c("12.4", "<5", "31.0")
crp  <- as.numeric(labs)
mean(crp, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```
Warning message:
NAs introduced by coercion
[1] 21.7
```

Did the code finish?

options.text: Yes — a warning lets R carry on, and the mean is 21.7
options.feedback:
Right. A warning isn't an error: R finishes, but flags that something
happened you might want to know about. Here, `"<5"` couldn't become a
number, so it turned into `NA` — and then `na.rm = TRUE` quietly left
it out. The mean is of 12.4 and 31.0 only.

Warnings sit between the two kinds of failure: the code ran, but R is
telling you something. They're easy to scroll past. Module 14 is about
problems that don't even warn you.

options.text: No — it stopped at the warning
options.feedback:
A warning never stops R. Only an error does. The `[1] 21.7` underneath
is the finished result.

options.text: Yes, and the mean includes all three values
options.feedback:
It finished, but not with all three. The warning says an `NA` was
introduced: `"<5"` couldn't become a number, and `na.rm = TRUE` then
left it out. 21.7 is the mean of 12.4 and 31.0.

title: Asking for help with an error
prompt:
You're stuck on an error you don't understand. Which of these gives a
search engine or an AI the best chance of helping?
hint: The message says what went wrong. What else would someone need to know?

options.text: The exact error message, plus the lines of code that produced it
options.feedback:
Right. The message says *what* went wrong; the code shows *where* and
*why*. With both, an AI can usually point at the line. For a search
engine, the message itself — in quotes, with "R" — finds other people
who hit the same thing.

Include the lines that feed the one R names, not just that line — as
the earlier exercise showed, the cause can sit a line or two above
where R noticed it.

One firm rule: share the code and the error, never real patient data.
If the problem depends on what the data looks like, describe its shape
— the column names and types — or make up a few rows with filler
values. And if you'd rather not reveal your variable names, to protect
an unpublished idea, say, swap them for placeholders like `col_a`.
Keep the message's wording and structure the same, and it'll still
work. Module 16 is about exactly this.

There's nothing here to go on. The error message is the most useful
thing you have — it says exactly what kind of problem it is.

options.text: The whole script, without the error message
options.feedback:
Better than nothing, but whoever's helping has to guess what went
wrong. The message tells them straight away.

options.text: Just the error message and the one line R says it's on
options.feedback:
Close, but the line R names is only where it *noticed* the problem. The
cause can sit a line or two above — like the quoted `height` earlier.
Include the lines that feed into the one R names.

title: A fix that hides the problem
prompt:
You pasted that warning into an AI, and it suggested this:

```r
crp <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(labs))
```

You run it, and the warning is gone. Is the problem fixed?
hint: Run it, then look at `crp`. What happened to `"<5"`?

options.text: No — the warning is hidden, but `"<5"` still becomes `NA` and gets dropped
options.feedback:
Right. `suppressWarnings()` does exactly what its name says: it stops
the warning being shown. It doesn't change what happened. `"<5"` still
becomes `NA`, and the mean still quietly leaves it out — you've just
lost the one sign that anything was wrong.

The real fix is a decision about `"<5"` — what number, if any, it
should become — and that's a clinical call, not a coding one.

It's a very common kind of suggestion, and a reasonable one to make if
you only see the warning and not what it's about. So when a fix makes
a warning or an error disappear, ask what it changed. If you see
`suppressWarnings()` in generated code, read it as a flag.

options.text: Yes — no warning means nothing went wrong
options.feedback:
Run it and look at `crp`: the middle value is still `NA`. The warning
was the only sign of that, and now it's hidden. Nothing about the data
changed.

It doesn't convert anything. It only stops the warning being printed.
`"<5"` still becomes `NA` — run it and look.
